To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

accumulation of gene alterations in human breast cancer occurs early in the process of tumorigenesis, and that the genotype and phenotype of breast cancer cells are determined mostly soon after the tumorigenic process.
the accumulation of gene alterations is a characteristic feature of the development of breast cancer, and that the accumulation is already evident at the preinvasion stage.

the c-erbB-2 gene is amplified in 30% of breast cancers, the p53 gene is mutated in 40-60% of breast cancers and that loss of heterozygosities on 16q are observed in 50% of invasive ductal carcinomas.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the accumulation of gene alterations in human breast cancer.
the accumulation of gene alterations and the progression of breast cancer.
the accumulation of gene alterations and their clinical implications.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the genetic changes in breast cancer are accumulated at the early stage, and the accumulation is associated with progression of cancer cells.
the genetic changes are the most important factors in the development of breast cancer, but that the environmental factors are not less important.
the genotype of breast cancer is determined relatively soon after tumorgenesis, and that the phenotype is acquired by accumulation of gene alterations during progression of breast cancer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetic alterations in human breast cancer occur in a step-wise manner and that the accumulation of the gene alterations would be responsible for the progression of breast cancer.
breast cancers are not heterogeneous at the genetic level.
the accumulation of gene alterations is an important mechanism of progression of breast cancer.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use a single cell to make many different measurements.

there is no single gene or pathway that drives the development of breast cancer, rather there are many genes and pathways that contribute to the disease, and these genes and pathways are not independent of each other.
there is a strong relationship between the number of gene mutations and the stage of the cancer.
